domains.title: Kami of Rice, Fertility, and Foxes
domains.subtitle: Guardian of the Harvest and Merchant Prosperity
domains.lead: Inari is one of the most widely worshipped kami in Japan: a deity of rice who became, over a thousand years, the patron of fertility, sake, smiths, merchants, and worldly success. The vermillion torii gates and fox statues of Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyōto are among the most iconic images of Japanese religion.

cards.name: Rice and Harvest
cards.desc: Inari governs the rice plant — enshrined as Uka-no-mitama, the spirit of the grain itself.

cards.name: Fox Messengers
cards.desc: Kitsune carry the kami's messages and hold the granary key in their statues' mouths.

cards.name: Merchant Success
cards.desc: From the medieval period, traders, brewers, and smiths prayed to Inari for prosperity.

cards.name: Fushimi Inari
cards.desc: The head shrine in Kyōto, founded in 711 CE, is ringed by mountains of donated torii.

symbols.name: Vermillion torii gates
symbols.meaning: The donated gates climbing Mount Inari — more than ten thousand — each one an invoice of a fulfilled prayer

symbols.name: Fox (kitsune)
symbols.meaning: The paired foxes flanking the shrine: one bears the granary key, one the jewel; red bibs mark their veneration

symbols.name: Rice sheaf
symbols.meaning: Inari's first body — the plant itself, worshipped as Uka-no-mitama before any temple existed

symbols.name: Jewel
symbols.meaning: The wish-granting gem in the fox's mouth; prosperity compressed to a single stone

symbols.name: Fried tofu (abura-age)
symbols.meaning: The offering said to please the fox — hence the sushi that bears Inari's name

mythology.lead: Inari has no single canonical myth cycle in the Kojiki manner. The kami's identity is distributed across a charter legend, a shifting triad of enshrined gods, the fox lore of the medieval period, and the craft legends of the cities — a biography written by worshippers rather than scribes.

myths.title: The Rice-Cake That Flew
myths.text: The Nihon Shoki (Wadō 4, 711 CE) tells how Hata no Irogu, a leader of the immigrant Hata clan, practiced archery on a mountain by setting up a rice-cake as a target. When his arrow struck it, the cake rose into the air as a white bird and flew to the summit, where a radiance appeared. Taking this as a divine sign, Irogu founded a shrine on the spot. Rice-cake, white bird, mountain light: the kami announced itself through its own substance. The Hata were continental immigrants — weavers, engineers, and shrine-builders — and their mountain cult folded the new rice technology into the older kami world. The date makes Inari's shrine among the oldest documented in Japan, and the legend is the charter of what became Fushimi Inari Taisha. It is already the whole theology of Inari — a deity who arrives riding the rice itself.

myths.title: Three Gods, One Kami
myths.text: At its head shrine, Inari is not one deity but three: Uka-no-mitama, the spirit of the rice plant; Satahiko; and Ōmiyanome, the ancestral weaver and food-goddess. Other Inari shrines substitute Toyouke, the goddess of the Ise Grand Shrine's outer precinct, who prepares the food of the gods. Medieval oracles ratified the triad, and the three remain enshrined today. Even the kami's gender never settled: Inari appears as an aged man, a radiant woman, or a fox-mounted deva, depending on the shrine and the century. Scholars read the fluidity as the mark of a genuinely popular cult, indifferent to the tidy genealogies of the court chronicles: Inari names less a person than an office, the power that fills the granary. The many-faced kami mirrors the many fates of rice — seedling, grain, sake, wealth — each a different disguise of one sustenance.

myths.title: The Messengers of the Granary
myths.text: By the medieval period the kitsune — the fox — had become Inari's recognized messenger, and by the Edo period Inari cult and fox cult were so entangled that temple regulations had to forbid offerings of fried tofu at certain times. Foxes carried the kami's messages, guarded the granary keys held in their statues' mouths, and appeared in dreams and possession cults. The thousands of vermillion torii at Fushimi Inari, each donated by a shop or a family, map the commercial empire of a deity whose messenger moves, like trade itself, silently at the margins of the night. In the fox, Inari acquired what few agricultural gods possess: a double, clever and dangerous, who could walk into the human world and speak with a human voice. Tales multiplied of fox-weddings glimpsed in the rain, of possessed mediums channeling the kami, and of the nine-tailed fox whose tails count its centuries.

myths.title: The Smith's Dream
myths.text: A tenth-century legend tells of Munechika, the Kyōto swordsmith ordered to forge a blade for the emperor with no partner to work the bellows. In a dream Inari promised help; a mysterious youth appeared, and before dawn two swords stood completed — one for the court, one kept by the smith. The tale, dramatized in the Nō play Kokaji, rests on the smith's dedication of his forge to Inari. The kami of the grain was equally the kami of the craft: rice becomes sake, and iron becomes a sword, by the same alchemy of transformation. The blades of the legend remain treasured names, and Munechika's Sanjō school of smiths flourished for generations at the capital. Inari's patronage of smiths, brewers, and merchants is the medieval extension of the oldest fact about the deity — that the stored harvest is capital, and capital wants a god.

lore.syncretism: Inari is the great syncret of Japanese religion. Medieval Tendai identified the kami with Dakiniten, the fox-riding deva absorbed from Indian tantra, and esoteric lineages placed Inari within mandala systems of the five grains. The Muromachi and Edo periods saw Inari conflated with Benzaiten and with Uka-no-mitama's Buddhist guises; fox-possession cults and Inari mediums blurred the shrine and the street. No figure in Japan tolerated layered identity more gracefully — male or female, one or three, kami or buddha. When the Meiji state ordered the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, Inari shrines quietly stored their Buddhist statuary away; most of it returned within a generation.
lore.culturalLegacy: Fushimi Inari Taisha, rebuilt after the Ōnin War and crowned with its endless gates, is among the most visited religious sites on earth, and the estimates of thirty thousand Inari shrines across Japan exceed any other deity's. The kami guards restaurants, rice merchants, and corporate headquarters; the sushi named for the fox, inari-zushi, is sold in every convenience store; and the fox-mask of festival stalls is recognizably Inari's. In a secular age, Inari prospers as the most pragmatic divinity in the pantheon: pray, work, and share the result — the god of the harvest became the god of the hustle.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Inari teaches that the sacred is not separate from the everyday. The rice in the bowl, the sake in the cup, the ledger of the shop, the contract of the marriage — all flow through one deity who declines to be a single person.

The fox is the perfect emblem of this theology: it crosses the boundary between field and village, animal and ancestor, omen and blessing, exactly as rice crosses from seed to wealth. To modern eyes Inari looks like a god of capitalism, and there is truth in it — Inari protected merchants when merchants were new, and prosperity cults follow prosperity. But the older lesson stands underneath: abundance is relational. The granary key is entrusted to a messenger, not a master, and the ten thousand gates are not a wall but an invitation.

lore.archaeology: Fushimi Inari Taisha in southern Kyōto has been Inari's head shrine since 711 CE. Burned in the Ōnin War (1468) and rebuilt by the late fifteenth century, its main halls, its tunnel-paths of donated torii — over ten thousand strong, dating chiefly from the Edo period onward — and the mountain-top okusha shrines form one of Japan's best-documented cult landscapes. Excavations and shrine records trace the cult's growth from a Hata-clan agricultural shrine to the devotional center of a national commercial network, and the thousands of subsidiary Inari shrines preserve medieval siting patterns at field boundaries and village entrances.
